Spent the day on Capitol Hill, which always leaves me with a brackish mix of hope over what we can be and despair over how far we are from our potential. Remember that we plant seeds today for trees whose shade we will not enjoy.

The data is clear: undocumented workers are deeply embedded in the U.S. economy. Policy decisions that ignore this reality carry real costs. 

Read the full analysis here
ageconsearch.umn.edu/record/…

For more: austinkocher.substack.com

Combined across agriculture, construction, hospitality, and other sectors, mass deportations affecting millions of workers could fuel inflation and reduce GDP, effects felt by every American household, not just immigrant communities.

If farm labor costs spike sharply, the consequences are straightforward: Americans pay more for domestically grown food, or the U.S. imports more fruits and vegetables from other countries. Neither outcome serves the stated goal of putting America first.

Mechanization is frequently offered as the solution, but current agricultural technologies are not efficient enough and are financially out of reach for many producers, especially for labor-intensive specialty crops.

Attracting domestic workers to farm jobs has proven unrealistic even during periods of high unemployment. The idea that Americans will fill these roles if undocumented workers are removed is not supported by historical evidence.

It's not just direct deportations that reduce labor supply. Research shows that even workers who aren't deported may reduce their hours out of fear of apprehension, an effect economists call "chilling effects" on labor supply.

The states with the largest undocumented populations (California, Texas, Florida, North Carolina, and Georgia) are also among the top five states for H-2A worker demand. Mass deportations would hit these agricultural regions especially hard.

Dairy, meatpacking, poultry, nurseries, and greenhouses are also heavily reliant on undocumented workers. The H-2A guest worker program largely excludes nonseasonal industries like dairy, leaving no easy legal replacement.

Agriculture is the sector most at risk. USDA data shows that at least 40% of the U.S. crop labor force has been undocumented in each of the last 30 years. This is not a marginal share, we are structurally dependent.

There are approximately 51.4 million foreign-born individuals in the U.S. Of those, 9.7 million have no legal protections and face the immediate possibility of deportation under current enforcement priorities.

It's impossible to avoid the economic effects of mass deportation. A new analysis in Choices Magazine breaks down what aggressive enforcement could mean for American workers, farmers, and your grocery bill. 🧵

Andrew Thrasher's full account of how this unfolded (the questions that remain, and what it means for schools) is essential reading. This is what independent, data-driven accountability journalism looks like in 2026. 

maxwellcommons.substack.com/…
Remember, someone dies every 6 days in a US detention facility. Learn the data, engage with it, share this thread, and demand a say over how your tax dollars are used.
Humanrightsfirst.org lets you track deportation and transfer flights of our detained population.

www.projectsaltbox.com features two very cool dudes who search through deeds and property info to track the land and warehouse space that ICE buys for future detention sites. From them we learn that ICE has spent 1 billion taxpayer dollars to create 40,000 beds so far.
Detentiondeaths.com is another outstanding citizen scholarship project tracking who has died in custody.  Of course, it cannot track those who are ill or injured, released, and die shortly after.
Detentionpregnancytracker.com tracks the pregnant women taken by ICE and what happens to them.
Enforcementdashboard.com is another great interface for some of this data.

Deportationdata.org is a project out of Berkeley that allows you to visualize data coming directly out of DHS own intake & processing systems. It isn't cleaned or interpreted, it's a by-product of immigration enforcement.

First check out detentionreports.com
to see how his team has leveraged FOIA to get the very best picture of what's going on.

Today the Spatial Histories Seminar at Vanderbilt hosted @austinkocher.com who collects and interprets US Immigration data. Here are some of his resources for you to get to better understand what's going on at DHS. 
🧵
